questions.question: Describe a crank, name its parts, and give four everyday examples.
questions.expected_answer: A crank is an arm fixed at right angles to the end of an axle or shaft with a handle or pin at the far end; turning the handle in a circle turns the axle. Parts: axle or shaft at the centre, crank arm, handle or crank pin, and the circle the pin traces. Examples: bicycle pedals, fishing reel handle, pencil sharpener, car window winder, hand drill, meat mincer, well windlass, borehole pump handle.

questions.question: Explain why a crank is described as an adaptation of a second-class lever, identifying the pivot, load and effort, and state what this means for its mechanical advantage.
questions.expected_answer: The pivot is the centre of the axle, the effort is the hand on the handle at the end of the crank arm, and the load is the resistance at the surface of the axle where it turns the gear or rope, a short distance from the centre. The load lies between the pivot and the effort, which is the second-class arrangement. The effort arm (crank arm length) is always longer than the load arm (axle radius), so the crank always gives a mechanical advantage of arm length divided by axle radius, and a longer arm gives a greater advantage.

questions.question: Describe the crank and slider mechanism, state the length of its stroke, and explain one way in which it differs from a cam.
questions.expected_answer: A connecting rod is joined to the crank pin at one end and to a slider at the other; the slider is held in a straight guide. As the crank turns, the pin moves in a circle and the rod pushes and pulls the slider back and forth, one full stroke per turn, with a stroke length of twice the crank arm. Driven from the slider end, as in an engine piston, it converts reciprocating motion to rotary. It differs from a cam in working in both directions with a smooth even stroke, whereas a cam converts rotary to reciprocating only and its follower's motion depends on the cam's shape.
